questions.hypothesis:
To set up a system to track your monthly expenses and stick to your $200 dining out budget, here is a recommended structure based on your tracking tools and budgeting strategies:

### 1. Structure Your Tracking System (Excel or YNAB)
* **Spreadsheet Layout**: Set up columns for **Category**, **Budgeted Amount**, **Actual Amount**, and **Difference**.
* **Core Categories**:
  * Housing ($1,200)
  * Utilities ($200)
  * Food / Groceries ($300)
  * Dining Out ($200)
  * Transportation ($100)
  * Entertainment ($150)
  * Miscellaneous ($50)
  * Emergency Fund ($216.67 – $433.33)
  * Medical Bills ($200)
  * Taxes ($200)
* **Log Expenses Consistently**: Record actual spending either daily or in weekly batches, using formulas or conditional formatting in Excel (or categories in YNAB) to flag when a category is nearing its limit.

---

### 2. Tactics to Stick to the $200 Dining Out Budget
* **Divide into Weekly Limits**: Break the $200 monthly allowance down to **$50 per week**. Tracking week-by-week makes overspending easier to catch early.
* **Use a Cash Envelope**: Withdraw $50 cash at the start of each week specifically for dining out. When the cash is gone, dining out stops until the next week.
* **Meal Planning & Batch Cooking**: 
  * Plan your weekly meals before grocery shopping to avoid impulse purchases.
  * Cook larger batches at home to have meals ready and pack lunches for work.
* **Choose Affordable Dining Options**: Target budget-friendly spots, utilize happy hour specials, or look for coupons/promotions when you do go out.

---

### 3. Check-ins & Alignment
* **Weekly/Monthly Reviews**: Schedule a regular check-in with Alexis to review transactions against the budget, discuss any upcoming expenses, and maintain financial transparency.
* **Adjust as Needed**: Review category totals at month-end to ensure dining out spending remains aligned with your broader savings and emergency fund milestones.

Your approach to managing finances with Alexis has evolved from basic expense tracking and initial compromise into structured collaboration, transparency, and joint goal-planning:

- **2020 – Early 2024 (Foundations & Daily Tracking):** You and Alexis began sharing household finances in 2020. By March 2024, while you generally aligned on large financial goals, day-to-day spending presented challenges. To address this, you instituted daily spending limits, regular check-ins, transparent sharing of receipts and Excel expense tracking, and agreed on a $200 monthly dining out budget starting in April.
- **May – June 2024 (Transparency & Compromise):** After experiencing stress around financial management, Alexis suggested opening a joint savings account at First National Bank to enhance transparency. When facing differing priorities—such as whether to invest $1,000 immediately or save it for a car—you reached a compromise by splitting the amount evenly ($500 to each).
- **September 2024 (Collaborative Goal-Setting & Budget Adjustments):** You deepened joint decision-making around new income, project scopes, and broader financial goals, including mutually agreeing to delay a vacation to 2025 to prioritize car savings. You also collaboratively revisited and increased your joint grocery budget from $400 to $500 per month.
- **December 2024 (Flexibility & Life Transition Support):** As Alexis prepared to launch a freelance business, your financial coordination shifted to accommodate life transitions, planning budget adjustments and trimming non-essential spending so you could reduce your work hours to 30 per week to provide support.
